extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claimed inventions satisfy 35 U.S.C. 101 subject matter eligibility, including claim construction (BRI), the Alice/Mayo two-part test, and related examination procedures. Focused on examiner steps, examples, and how to formulate and support §101 rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two criteria for subject matter eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: First, the claimed invention must be to one of the four statutory categories. Second, the claimed invention must qualify as patent-eligible subject matter, i.e., the claim must not be directed to a judicial exception unless the claim as a whole includes additional limitations amounting to significantly more than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial exceptions are abstract ideas, laws of nature, and natural phenomena (including products of nature). Integration of an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon into a practical application may be eligible. See Alice/Mayo framework for determining whether additional limitations amount to 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Four statutory categories (35 U.S.C. 101)
rubrics_metrics.description: The four categories are processes, machines, manufactures and compositions of matter. Processes define 'actions' (a series of steps); the latter three define physical or tangible 'things' or 'products.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When determining whether a claim falls in one of these categories, verify that the invention is claimed in a physical or tangible form for machines/manufactures/compositions. Non-limiting non-statutory examples include data per se, computer program per se (product-type claims without structural recitations), transitory signals, and subject matter expressly prohibited (e.g., humans per se).

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of claim as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: It is essential that the BRI of the claim be established prior to examining a claim for eligibility; the BRI sets the boundaries of coverage sought and influences whether the claim seeks to cover non-statutory subject matter or is directed to a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim interpretation affects both Step 1 (statutory category) and Step 2 (Alice/Mayo). Examples: Mentor Graphics (BRI covered non-statutory carrier waves) and Synopsys/Enfish (claim construction affected whether claims were considered mental steps or technological improvements). If BRI covers statutory and non-statutory embodiments, the claim may fail Step 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo two-part test (Step 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2A: Determine whether the claims are directed to an abstract idea, a law of nature, or a natural phenomenon (a judicial exception). Step 2B: If so, determine whether the claim recites additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception (the 'search for an inventive concept').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Alice/Mayo two-part test is the only test to evaluate eligibility under §101. Consider machine-or-transformation and other clues as part of the 'integration' or 'significantly more' analysis, not as a separate test. Courts have described Step 2B as looking for an 'inventive concept.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Flowchart pathways A, B, and C (streamlined/standard analyses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pathway A: Claims that fall within a statutory category and whose eligibility is self-evident may be found eligible using a streamlined analysis. Pathway B: Claims that fall within a statutory category and are not directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) are eligible at Pathway B. Pathway C: Claims that fall within a statutory category, are directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES), and recite additional elements that amount to significantly more (Step 2B: YES) are eligible at Pathway C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If uncertain whether streamlined analysis is appropriate, the examiner is encouraged to conduct a full eligibility analysis. Claims not eligible under any pathway should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility Step 1: whether a claim is to a statutory category
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1 asks: Is the claim to a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter? Evaluation should be made after reviewing the entire disclosure and construing the claims under BRI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A process is a series of acts; machines/manufactures/compositions must have physical or tangible form. For product claims, verify presence of structural/physical limitations. Examples of non-statutory product claims include intangible collections of information and software detached from any medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: BRI covering statutory and non-statutory embodiments — consequences and remediation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the BRI of a claim covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments, the claim embraces non-statutory subject matter, fails Step 1, and should be rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice: point out the BRI and recommend an amendment narrowing the claim to statutory embodiments if possible. Use appropriate form paragraphs (e.g., 7.05, 7.05.01) when making a §101 rejection for lack of statutory subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility Step 2A: whether a claim is directed to a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2A determines whether a claim is directed to an abstract idea, natural phenomenon, or law of nature. Claims that are directed to nothing more than such exceptions are not eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to case law (Alice, Mayo, Diehr, Benson, Flook, Bilski) in identifying judicial exceptions. If claim is directed to a judicial exception proceed to Step 2B; if not, claim is eligible without Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract ideas: groupings and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract ideas include certain methods of organizing human activity, mental processes, mathematical concepts/formulas, and other concepts courts have identified as abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP provides example lists and 'tentative abstract ideas' to guide examiners. Determine whether claimed steps are mere mental steps, mathematical formulas, or other abstract groupings; consider whether claim limitations meaningfully integrate the idea into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of nature, natural phenomena, and products of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to laws of nature, natural phenomena, and products of nature are judicial exceptions and are not eligible unless the claim as a whole integrates them into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate product-of-nature claims under the 'markedly different characteristics' analysis to decide if the claimed subject matter has sufficient human-made distinction from its natural counterpart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics analysis (product-of-nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: A product of nature is patent-ineligible unless the claimed subject matter has 'markedly different characteristics' from the naturally occurring counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess structure, function, and properties compared to naturally occurring form. If the claimed subject matter exhibits markedly different characteristics due to human modification, it may not be a product of nature and may pass Step 2A consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of a judicial exception into a practical application (Step 2A prong two)
rubrics_metrics.description: Integration of an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon into a practical application can weigh against a conclusion that the claim is directed to a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of integration that can show practical application include improvements to computer functionality or other technologies (see 2106.04(d)(1)) and particular treatment or prophylaxis in medical methods (see 2106.04(d)(2)). Consider whether claim limitations apply the exception in a meaningful way to produce a technical solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility Step 2B: whether the claim amounts to significantly more (inventive concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2B evaluates whether additional claim elements, individually or in combination, provide 'significantly more' than the judicial exception — i.e., an inventive concept that transforms the claim into patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors/considerations include: (a) improvements to the functioning of a computer or other technology, (b) particular machine, (c) particular transformation, (d) well-understood, routine, conventional activity (negative factor), (e) other meaningful limitations, (f) mere instructions to apply an exception (negative), (g) insignificant extra-solution activity (negative), and (h) field of use or technological environment. Evaluate whether claimed limitations are conventional or amount to a technical contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis (2106.06): eligibility is self-evident or clear technology improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: When eligibility is self-evident or the claim demonstrates a clear improvement to technology or computer functionality, a streamlined analysis (Pathway A) may be appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If uncertain whether streamlined analysis is appropriate, conduct the full two-part Alice/Mayo analysis. Claims that would be eligible under Pathway A but subjected to Steps 2A/2B should ultimately be found eligible at Pathway B or C if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulating and supporting §101 rejections; evaluating applicant responses (2106.07)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on preparing proper §101 rejections, using form paragraphs, supporting factual and legal reasoning, and how to evaluate and respond to applicant arguments and amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specified form paragraphs when a Step 1 rejection is appropriate. When making a §101 rejection, complete examination under other patentability statutes (35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112) should still be made. Evaluate applicant responses on the merits and clarify the record as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on superseded or incorrect tests or utility as the eligibility metric
rubrics_metrics.description: The MPEP emphasizes that certain prior tests are superseded or should not be used as the basis for eligibility determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not evaluate eligibility based on whether the claim recites a 'useful, concrete, and tangible result' (State Street/Alappat era test) or on 'utility' (utility is not the test for §101). The machine-or-transformation test is an important clue but not a separate test. The 'special purpose computer' rationale (In re Alappat) has been superseded by Bilski and Alice.

rubrics_metrics.name: §101 is a threshold inquiry; use §102, §103, §112 and other provisions as tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners are reminded that 35 U.S.C. 101 is only a threshold test; other statutes (35 U.S.C. 112, 35 U.S.C. 102, 35 U.S.C. 103) provide additional tools to ensure claimed inventions meet conditions for patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a claim is eligible under §101, it must still be novel, nonobvious, and meet written-description/enablement requirements. Conversely, a §101 rejection does not obviate examining other statutory requirements during prosecution.
